paragraphs.text: The continued popularity of the functional approach to describe what managers do is a tribute to its clarity and simplicity. According to the functional approach, managers a) plan. b) organize c) lead and d) control through a series of ongoing and continuous decisions and work activities. But does that accurately describe what all managers really do? One prominent management researcher, Henry Mintzberg, would say no, arguing that what manager do is best described by looking at the roles they play at work.

In the late 1960s, Mintzberg made a detailed study of five top managers at work. What he discovered challenged several long-held notions about the managers job. For instance. In contrast to the predominant views at the time that managers were reflective thinkers who carefully and systematically processed information before making decisions, Mintzberg found that his managers engaged in a large number of varied, unpatterned and short-duration activities. Managers had little time for reflective thinking because they encountered constant interruptions. Half of their activities lasted less than nine minutes each. In addition to these insights, Minteberg provided a categorization scheme for defining what managers do based on observations of their work. Mintzberg concluded that managers perform ten different but highly interrelated roles. These can be called decision-making roles.

In category I, all managers are required to perform duties that involve people (subordinates and persons outside the organisation) and other duties that are ceremonial and symbolic in nature. These are the interpersonal roles. When the dean of a university hands out degrees at graduation or a factory supervisor gives a group of high school students a plant tour, they are acting in a figurehead role. All managers also have a role as a leader. This role includes hiring, training, motivating and disciplining employees. The third role within the interpersonal grouping is the liaison role. Mintzberg describes this activity as contacting external sources who provide the manager with information. These sources are individuals or groups outside the managers unit and maybe inside or outside the organisation. The sales manager who obtains information from the human resources manager in the same company has an internal liaison relationship. When that sales manager confers with other sales executives at a marketing trade association meeting, he or she has an outside liaison relationship.

Next, in category II, all managers, to some degree, have informational roles. receiving, collecting and disseminating information. Typically, if they are getting this information from outside their own organisation. They do so by reading magazines and talking with others to learn what competitors may be planning. and so on. Mintzberg called this the ‘monitor’ role. Managers also act as channels of information to organisational members. This is the ‘disseminator’ role. When they represent the organisation to outsiders, managers perform a spokesperson role.

Finally, in category III, Mintzberg identified four decisional roles, which revolve around making choices. As entrepreneurs, managers initiate and oversee new projects that will improve their organisation's performance. As disturbance handlers, managers take corrective action in response to unforeseen problems. As resource allocators, managers are responsible for allocating human, physical and monetary resources. Managers also perform as negotiators when they discuss and bargain with other groups to gain advantages for their own units.

A number of follow-up studies have tested the validity of Mintzberg's role categories. The evidence generally supports the idea that managers regardless of the type of organization or level within the organization perform similar roles. However, the emphasis that managers give to the various roles seems to change with their organisational level. Specifically, the roles of ‘disseminator’, figurehead liaison and spokesperson are more important at the higher levels of the organisation than at the lower ones. Conversely, the leader role is more important for lower-level manager than it is for either middle-or top-level managers.
Have these managerial roles invalidated the traditional functions of planning, organising, lending and controlling? Definitely not!

First, the functional approach still represents the most useful way of conceptualising the manager's job. One management journal states that: ‘The classical functions provide clear discrete methods of classifying the thousands of activities that managers carry out.’ Second, although Mintzberg offers a more elaborate classification scheme of what managers do, these roles can be substantially reconciled with the four functions. For instance, resource allocation and the entrepreneurial role are part of planning, and all of the interpersonal roles are part of the leading function. Although most of Mintzberg's other roles fit into one or more of the four functions, not all of them do, that is because all managers do some work that is not purely managerial Mintzberg's observation of time spent in public relations or raising money shows that not all managerial activities are an essential part of the manager's job classifications may include some activities that should not have been included.
Do these comments mean that Mintzberg's role categories are invalid? Not at all!

Mintzberg clearly offered new insights into what managers do. The attention his work has received is evidence of the importance attributed to defining management roles. Management is still a relatively young, evolving discipline. Future research comparing and integrating Mintzberg's roles with the four functions will continue to expand our understanding of the manager's job.
